_readme: THE AUTOMATIONS A PERSON ALREADY HAS, before meeting Sailor: the hooks of a
command line, the operating system's services, the scheduled tasks, the
scattered scripts. It is the list the system flow «migrate-to-sailor»
works on, and it is data like everything else: rewrite it, extend it or
switch it off without recompiling anything.
To add one: put a `.json` file in `~/.config/sailor/tools.d/` holding an
array of descriptors, and ask for it with `descriptor_paths` in the step. An
`id` already present in here is replaced by yours; to remove one, rewrite its
`id` with `"disabled": true`.
IT LIVES IN A CATALOG SEPARATE FROM THE TOOLS, AND NOT FOR TIDINESS. Someone
else's automation is not something a flow step can invoke: in the same list
as the tools, its identifier would appear among the ones Sailor offers to
whoever mistyped a name, and a flow could name it as if it were a binary to
run.
NO ENTRY HERE DECLARES `version`, AND THAT IS A RULE OF THE CATALOG. Asking
for a version means running a binary: this list looks at the personal
configuration of whoever runs it, and looking must never mean starting
something.
THE FOUR FAMILIES CARRY THE VERDICT, and the flow shows them apart:
`automation_hook` — starts when something happens; in Sailor it would be a
trigger plus a flow. `automation_schedule` — starts at a time or on an
interval; in Sailor it would be a flow's schedule. `automation_script` — a
program somebody runs by hand; in Sailor it would be a step, but nobody can
say when it runs, and that «when» is written nowhere.
`automation_opaque` — found, and not readable with today's tools.
IT LOOKS IN THE USER'S HOME, not in the project. A flow can be launched from
a window started who knows where, and a wrong working directory would tell
someone with twelve hooks that they have none.

tools.label: Claude Code hooks, valid everywhere
tools.note: The entries are the event names (PreToolUse, Stop, SessionStart…). Each runs a command: in Sailor that would be a trigger with that name plus a flow doing what the command does. Today Sailor has only one trigger source that really works — the manual one — so the translation can be read, not run.

tools.label: Claude Code hooks declared project by project
tools.note: They are read from home and not from the project, because home is what keeps the list: that way the projects nobody is working on right now are visible too.

tools.label: hooks declared for the Claude application
tasks declared for the editor
tools.note: The entries under `tasks` are an array, not an object: if nothing shows up here although tasks exist, that is why, and the repair belongs in the descriptor.

tools.label: the user's launchd services (macOS)
tools.note: One file per service. Inside is the command and, when scheduled, `StartInterval` or `StartCalendarInterval`: those would be a flow's recurrence. Sailor does not read plists today — it is XML, and there is no reader — so the names show here, not what they do.

tools.label: machine-wide launchd services (macOS)
tools.note: Installed by other programs for every user: look, do not touch.

tools.label: system launchd daemons (macOS)
tools.note: They run outside the user's session, often as root. They are not material to migrate into a flow: they are in the list because whoever asks «what starts by itself on this machine» has to see them.

tools.label: the user's systemd units (Linux)
tools.note: A `.timer` is the recurrence, the `.service` is what runs. The pair is the closest thing to a scheduled Sailor flow that exists on an ordinary machine.

tools.label: the user's cron table
tools.note: CAREFUL, A «NOT HERE» MEANS NOTHING HERE: on nearly every system these directories are readable only by root, and the honest way to ask is `crontab -l`, which is a command to run — something this list never does. If you have cron jobs, look at them with `crontab -l` and carry them over by hand.

tools.label: the system cron jobs dropped into a directory
tools.note: These read without privileges almost everywhere, unlike the personal table.

tools.label: the scripts in the personal directories of the search path
tools.note: A program somebody runs by hand. In Sailor it would be a step, and the translation is immediate; what is missing is the «when», which is written nowhere — hence a family of their own, and not the scheduled one.

tools.label: the files the shell runs at startup
tools.note: Inside are aliases, functions and hooks that are automations in all but name. Sailor does not read them and must not: reading them would mean interpreting the shell, and an interpreter inside Sailor is exactly what the project forbids. All that is said here is that they exist.

tools.label: the Codex configuration
tools.note: It is TOML, and Sailor has no TOML reader: you see that the file is there, not what it declares. Mind which file counts, too: CODEX_HOME can move it, and the one you read by hand is not always the one its host uses.

tools.label: the git hooks of your repositories
tools.note: THERE IS A DECLARED GAP HERE, and it is worth knowing about instead of believing it covered. The real hooks live in `.git/hooks` inside each repository, and this list looks at home, not at the projects; on top of that every new repository puts thirteen `.sample` files there which never run, and a `*` pattern cannot exclude them. Listing them would give thirteen lines of noise per repository. Only the shared hooks directory shows, if you configured one with `core.hooksPath`.
